articles.title: The Biglaw Firm That Rode The Dot-Com Wave All The Way To The Bottom
articles.content:
Ed. Note: Welcome to our daily feature Trivia Question of the Day!

Which nearly 80-year-old San Francisco firm became the hottest law shop of the dot-com boom, handling hundreds of tech IPOs and sometimes even taking equity stakes in the startups it represented instead of cash, it nearly doubled in size, to roughly 900 lawyers, in just a few years. But when the bubble burst things came crashing down — its tech clients cratered (some into bankruptcy), a star chairman led a wave of partners out the door, and a last-ditch merger (with Morgan Lewis) collapsed. In January 2003, the partners voted to shut it down, throwing some 1,100 people out of work across 14 offices — the defining law firm casualty of the dot-com crash.

Hint: Founded in 1926, it was long one of San Francisco’s most prestigious firms. Its ousted chairman, Tower Snow, decamped to Clifford Chance with a group of partners. A Slate headline summed up its demise as “The Dot-Firm’s Dot-Bomb.”

See the answer on the next page.

The post The Biglaw Firm That Rode The Dot-Com Wave All The Way To The Bottom appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: If You Want Business Contacts To Remember You, Consider Giving Gifts In November
articles.content:
For most professionals whose businesses rely on word-of-mouth and referrals, strong relationships are the foundation of sustained success. The most common way to maintain or rekindle those connections is by sending thoughtful holiday cards or gifts. Yet the vast majority of people wait until early December to do so. That timing creates unnecessary competition, stress, and diminished impact. To avoid this, consider shopping and sending gifts in November.
December quickly turns chaotic. Shoppers compete for limited parking, often ending up blocks away from stores. Popular items sell out fast, forcing last-minute substitutions or markups on secondary markets. Even online orders face the risk of delays during peak shipping periods. Meanwhile, the calendar fills with holiday parties, family obligations, and end-of-year work deadlines that leave little time for careful selection. The result is often rushed, impersonal gifts that blend into the seasonal noise.
Sending gifts in November is unexpected but it could work. First, an early gift stands out. By late November and into December, inboxes and doorsteps overflow with cards and packages. Recipients are frequently distracted by parties, shopping, and travel plans, so many gestures receive only fleeting attention or get overlooked entirely. A well-timed November gift arrives when the holiday rush has not yet fully begun, making it more memorable and more likely to be genuinely appreciated.
Second, November opens a natural opportunity for edible gifts. Gift baskets filled with wine, cheese, meats, candies, or other treats can become part of a recipient’s Thanksgiving celebration. Because Thanksgiving is a broadly observed secular holiday in the United States, this timing feels inclusive and thoughtful rather than tied to any single religious or cultural tradition that dominates December. Your gift gains an extra layer of relevance and warmth simply by aligning with an existing gathering.
Third, shopping in November is simply less stressful. There are no Black Friday crowds, fewer Cyber Monday shipping bottlenecks, and a much higher chance that popular items remain in stock at regular prices. Your schedule is also freer: fewer competing holiday parties and family events mean you can take time to choose gifts with real consideration instead of defaulting to the same generic item for everyone. Thoughtfulness becomes practical rather than aspirational.
In short, shifting gift-giving to November not only shows appreciation to the people you collaborate with, it allows you to stand out. Early gifts cut through the noise, connect meaningfully with Thanksgiving, and free you from the December scramble. For professionals who understand that relationships drive referrals and reputation, this small change in timing could deliver a better return on investment: less stress for you, greater impact for the people who matter to your business, and stronger connections that last well beyond the season.
Steven Chung is a tax attorney in Los Angeles, California. He helps people with basic tax planning and resolve tax disputes. He is also sympathetic to people with large student loans. He can be reached via email at stevenchungatl@gmail.com. Or you can connect with him on Twitter (@stevenchung) and connect with him on LinkedIn.

articles.title: AI Connectors For E-Discovery: Great To Drive, But There Are Speed Limits
articles.content:
A recent article reminded me again of the dangers of unfettered use of AI tools, particularly by business employees. Employees who mistakenly believe that what they put in and get out is private. It’s not.
According to the article, Reveal announced that its Onna platform can now collect conversations and other materials that employees generate in Claude Enterprise. Reveal provides AI platforms for e-discovery purposes; among other things, Onna already provided similar capabilities for users of ChatGPT and Gemini. And other e-discovery providers offer similar tools. This means that the prompts employees write and what those prompts generate can now be easily searched and collected for review.
The idea, of course, is that it will help businesses and their lawyers respond to discovery requests more efficiently and accurately. Or be able to easily obtain and review this material for internal investigations.
A Wake-Up Call
No doubt this is all true and provides a good tool. But it’s also a good reminder for in-house legal departments. I fear that lots of employees are using Claude and other AI tools for all sorts of things, thinking that what they put in there is, well, private.
For legal and discovery purposes, this lack of understanding could be disastrous. If employees don’t understand that whatever they put in Claude could be discoverable, they could be creating all sorts of “smoking guns.” Documents that, at the very least, could be hard to explain.
Of course, that was true before Onna came along, and its integration doesn’t make that risk any greater than it always was. But it’s an important reminder that all the AI stuff that goes in and comes out may be discoverable. Which your employees may not appreciate.
It underscores your responsibility for employee education and training, as I have discussed before. It’s like the early days of email. I saw too many instances of hard-to-explain emails coming to light in litigation. All because employees didn’t realize that their emails were discoverable. Or fully appreciate that fact. Employees indeed need to understand litigation, its dangers and costs. And the parameters of discovery.
The ‘Private’ File
I had a case one time where we spent considerable time pulling together the documents and materials for production. I just happened to ask one key employee at the tail end of the process if we had everything. He sort of shrugged and said he guessed so. Then he added, “You got everything but the private file I keep on my home computer.” Crap. Of course, that “private file” contained all sorts of notes and data that were highly relevant to the case.
The point is that in-house and outside counsel can’t assume that employees know the risks without some education. Without some time being spent in training.
And believe me, that’s time well spent. You reduce the risk of bad documents being inadvertently created that could adversely affect the outcome. And think of this: you will also reduce your legal spend. Take it from me, your lawyers will spend countless hours dealing with documents that should never have been created. Or at least never worded the way they were.
An Exponential Danger
And this danger grows exponentially when you start thinking about the use of AI. It’s so easy and tempting to use for anything and everything. You often don’t think twice about what you put in it. And because it’s so conversational, it’s easy to add things and play around with prompts in ways that could be hard to explain later. It’s easy to forget you aren’t talking to a human. It’s easy to forget you’re making a record.
Sure, you may be able to later argue that some of this stuff might, and I emphasize might, be protected by the attorney-client or work product privileges. But the law here is unsettled.
And the work product privilege is not absolute in any event. To be honest, I would much rather not have documents around that I have to hope are covered by it.
It’s also a good reminder that what employees put into AI using their own devices can also be discoverable. Their cell phones. Their home laptops. There are no private files when it comes to litigation.
It Belongs To The Company
There’s another issue here that I almost hate to bring up. Generally, anything an employee puts into a work platform belongs to the company. And the company is usually entitled to access that material any time it wants. I know that. In-house legal knows that. But do your employees all know that?
Education about AI and the lack of privacy is a good time to reinforce the point that employers have the right to see what employees put in and take out of the employer’s AI systems. It might save heartburn all the way around if this were specifically covered when you talk to them about litigation risks.
Training Need Not Be Hard
And the training and education need not be all that difficult. I used to give a couple of sessions a year to good clients and their employees about how not to create bad documents but still do their job. I would throw in a few examples from real well-known cases that more than made the point. For in-house counsel, I can tell you your outside lawyers would be more than happy to do similar sessions at no charge. If they’re worth their salt and business savvy, that is.
Obey The Speed Limit
So it’s great that companies like Reveal come up with tools that make the e-discovery process more efficient and less time-consuming. It would be even better if the searches these tools enable didn’t turn up prejudicial and embarrassing materials. That would be a win-win.
But if you want that win-win, you’ve got to take time to educate your workforce about the shiny new AI tool. A tool that’s great for them to drive, but you sure don’t want them going 100 mph. In a school zone.
Stephen Embry is a lawyer, speaker, blogger, and writer. He publishes TechLaw Crossroads, a blog devoted to the examination of the tension between technology, the law, and the practice of law.
The post AI Connectors For E-Discovery: Great To Drive, But There Are Speed Limits appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: AI May Speed Up Legal Research, But That Doesn’t Automatically Shrink The Bill
articles.content:
Ed. note: Welcome to our daily feature, Quote of the Day.
Plaintiffs have not shown that defense counsel’s use of AI rendered the hours that they actually expended unreasonable.
— Judge Carolyn McHugh, writing for a unanimous Tenth Circuit panel, affirming a $114,663.11 fee award to Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck after Flux Drive’s trade secrets suit was dismissed. Flux Drive argued the firm’s use of AI and online research tools should have reduced its fees, but the court said the company pointed to no specific inflated billing entry. The panel acknowledged AI may reduce research time, while noting that lawyers still must verify their authorities and arguments. Brownstein partner Christopher Ottele welcomed the ruling, saying AI “is not a substitute for the judgment and analysis that attorneys still must exercise” in court filings.
Staci Zaretsky is the managing editor of Above the Law, where she’s worked since 2011. She’d love to hear from you, so please feel free to email her with any tips, questions, comments, or critiques. You can follow her on Bluesky, X/Twitter, and Threads, or connect with her on LinkedIn.
